title: Representation Count f(n)
content: The function $f(n)$ counts the number of ways to write $n = p + a$ where $p$ is prime and $a \in A$. Formally, it is the cardinality of the set of pairs $(p, a)$ with $p$ prime, $a \in A$, and $p + a = n$. This is the central object of Problem #237 — the question is whether $f(n)$ can stay bounded or must become arbitrarily large.
mathContext: $f_A(n) = |\{(p, a) : p \text{ prime},\; a \in A,\; p + a = n\}| = \sum_{\substack{a \in A \\ a < n}} \mathbf{1}_{n-a \text{ prime}}$

title: Logarithmic Lower Density
content: A set $A$ has logarithmic lower density if $|A \cap \{1, \ldots, N\}| \ge c \cdot \log N$ for some constant $c > 0$ and all sufficiently large $N$. This is a very weak density condition — much weaker than positive lower density. For example, the powers of two $\{1, 2, 4, 8, \ldots\}$ have logarithmic density since $|\{2^k : 2^k \le N\}| = \lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor + 1 \sim \log N / \log 2$.
mathContext: $\text{HasLogDensity}(A) \iff \exists c > 0,\; \exists N_0,\; \forall N \ge N_0: |A \cap [1, N]| \ge c \log N$. This implies $A$ is infinite but is much weaker than $|A \cap [1,N]| \gg N^\epsilon$ for any $\epsilon > 0$.

title: Unbounded Limsup
content: The predicate $\text{HasUnboundedLimsup}(f)$ means $\forall M,\; \exists n,\; f(n) > M$, which is equivalent to $\limsup_{n \to \infty} f(n) = \infty$. Note this does not require $f(n) \to \infty$; it only requires that $f(n)$ exceeds any bound infinitely often. There may still be values of $n$ where $f(n) = 0$.

title: Erdős's Original Conjecture
content: Erdős conjectured that if $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has logarithmic lower density, then the representation count $f_A(n)$ has unbounded limsup. This asks whether a very sparse set — growing only as fast as $\log N$ — is still dense enough to produce unbounded prime-plus-set representations. The answer is yes, and much more is true.

title: Chen-Ding Stronger Version
content: Chen and Ding (2022) proved a dramatically stronger result: any infinite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has unbounded representation count — not just sets with logarithmic density. Since logarithmic density implies infinitude, this immediately implies Erdős's conjecture. The strengthening is substantial: an infinite set can grow arbitrarily slowly (e.g., $A = \{2^{2^{2^k}} : k \ge 0\}$), yet still has unbounded $f_A(n)$.

title: Powers of Two
content: The set $A = \{2^k : k \ge 0\} = \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, \ldots\}$. This is a canonical example of a set with logarithmic density: $|A \cap [1, N]| = \lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor + 1$. It was the first set for which Erdős established the unbounded limsup property (1950).
mathContext: $A = \{2^k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$. Then $|A \cap [1, N]| = \lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor + 1$ and $f_A(n) = |\{k : n - 2^k \text{ is prime}\}|$.

title: Erdős 1950 Result
content: Erdős (1950) proved that for $A = \{2^k\}$, the representation count $f(n) = |\{k : n - 2^k \text{ is prime}\}|$ has unbounded limsup. His proof used sieve methods and properties of primes in arithmetic progressions. This was the motivating special case that led to the general conjecture.
mathContext: $\limsup_{n \to \infty} |\{k \ge 0 : n - 2^k \text{ is prime}\}| = \infty$. The proof uses the fact that for each $n$, the values $n - 2^k$ for $k = 0, 1, \ldots, \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ lie in distinct residue classes modulo small primes.

title: Chen and Ding 2022 Theorem
content: Chen and Ding (2022) proved that EVERY infinite set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has unbounded representation count. Their proof combines the Prime Number Theorem with a careful pigeonhole argument: among the infinitely many elements of $A$, sufficiently many must have prime complements $n - a$ for suitable $n$. The key innovation was removing any density hypothesis entirely.
mathContext: $\forall A \subseteq \mathbb{N},\; |A| = \infty \implies \forall M,\; \exists n,\; f_A(n) > M$. This is axiomatized as the StrongerVersion predicate.

title: Original Conjecture is True
content: The original Erdős conjecture follows from the Chen-Ding theorem via a simple logical reduction: a set with logarithmic density is infinite (if it were finite, $|A \cap [1,N]|$ would be bounded, contradicting $|A \cap [1,N]| \ge c \log N \to \infty$). The proof has one sorry for the finite-set-can't-have-log-density technicality, which would require showing that a finite subset of $\mathbb{N}$ is bounded above.
mathContext: $\text{HasLogDensity}(A) \implies |A| = \infty \implies \limsup f_A(n) = \infty$. The first implication uses $c \log N \to \infty$; the second is Chen-Ding.

title: Prime Number Theorem Connection
content: The Prime Number Theorem — $\pi(n) \sim n/\log n$ — is the engine behind the Chen-Ding result. Among the integers $\{n - a : a \in A,\; a < n\}$, the PNT ensures that a positive proportion are prime. As $n$ grows and $A$ is infinite, more elements of $A$ fall below $n$, generating more candidate pairs $(p, a)$ with $p + a = n$.
mathContext: By PNT, $\pi(n) \sim n/\log n$. For large $n$ and $a \in A$ with $a < n$, the 'probability' that $n - a$ is prime is roughly $1/\log(n-a) \approx 1/\log n$. Summing over the $|A \cap [1, n)|$ elements gives heuristic $f_A(n) \approx |A \cap [1,n)| / \log n$.

title: Squares Example
content: The set of perfect squares $A = \{1, 4, 9, 16, \ldots\}$ is infinite, so by Chen-Ding, $\limsup f_A(n) = \infty$. Concretely, $f_A(n) = |\{k \ge 1 : n - k^2 \text{ is prime}\}|$. The squares have density $\sim \sqrt{N}$ in $[1, N]$, far exceeding logarithmic density.
mathContext: $A = \{k^2 : k \ge 1\}$, $|A \cap [1, N]| = \lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor$. Then $f_A(n) = |\{k : 1 \le k^2 < n,\; n - k^2 \text{ prime}\}|$.

title: Prime Powers Example
content: The set of prime powers $A = \{p^k : p \text{ prime},\; k \ge 1\}$ is infinite. By Chen-Ding, it has unbounded representation count. This connects to questions about expressing integers as sums of a prime and a prime power, studied in analytic number theory via the Hardy-Littlewood circle method.
mathContext: $A = \{p^k : p \text{ prime},\; k \ge 1\}$. By PNT, $|A \cap [1, N]| = \pi(N) + \pi(N^{1/2}) + \cdots \sim N/\log N$.

title: Goldbach Connection
content: This problem belongs to the family of binary additive problems $n = p + a$ where $a$ ranges over a structured set. When $A = \{\text{primes}\}$, this becomes the Goldbach conjecture ($n = p_1 + p_2$). When $A = \{k^2\}$, it asks about primes plus squares (Waring-Goldbach). The Chen-Ding result is notable because it works for any infinite $A$, not requiring any arithmetic structure.
mathContext: Binary additive problem: $n = p + a$ with $a \in A$. Special cases: $A = \{\text{primes}\}$ gives Goldbach; $A = \{k^2\}$ gives primes-plus-squares; $A = \{2^k\}$ gives Erdős's 1950 case.

title: Erdős Problem #237 SOLVED
content: The main theorem `erdos_237` states that the original conjecture is true: $\text{ErdosConjecture}$ holds. It is defined as an alias for `erdos_conjecture_true`, which reduces to Chen-Ding via the log-density-implies-infinite argument. The answer to Problem #237 is YES.

title: Summary Theorem
content: The summary theorem packages both results: the original Erdős conjecture is true AND the stronger Chen-Ding version (infinite sets suffice) is also true. This gives the complete picture: not only is the answer YES, but the hypothesis can be dramatically weakened from logarithmic density to mere infinitude.
